cards.front: Four good reasons to go multi-agent
cards.back: Context isolation, parallelism, different tools or permissions per agent, and independent checking. Split by context, not by job title.

cards.front: Token cost of agents and multi-agent systems
cards.back: Anthropic reported agents use about 4× the tokens of a chat and its multi-agent research system about 15×. The task has to be worth it.
In tightly coupled work where each step needs everything the last step saw, such as most edits inside one codebase. Workers can't run in parallel and each loses detail.
One lead agent plans, briefs workers that run with their own context and tools, often in parallel, then merges their reports. Workers never talk to each other or to the user.

cards.front: Five parts of a worker brief
cards.back: Objective, output format, tools and sources, boundaries (what it does not own) and an effort budget. A vague brief is the most common supervisor failure.
A simple fact needs one agent and 3 to 10 tool calls; a comparison 2 to 4 workers with 10 to 15 calls each; complex research more than 10 workers with divided scopes.
Agents call each other directly and each decides who goes next. Flexible for open-ended work, but needs a hop limit, a termination condition and one owner of the answer.
Supervisors of supervisors, for jobs too big for one supervisor's context. Each layer summarises, so detail fades and cost and latency add up per layer.
The active agent transfers the conversation and its ownership to a specialist, usually through a tool like transfer_to_billing. Only one agent works at a time and it talks to the user directly.

Message passing sends explicit briefs and reports, so each agent sees only what it was sent. Shared state (a blackboard) lets every agent read and write one object, which risks lost updates and bloat.

cards.front: Preventing lost updates in shared state
cards.back: Append with a reducer, give each worker its own key, or use message passing instead of read-modify-overwrite.
Deduplicate while keeping sources, resolve conflicts on evidence (primary, newer, with conditions), carry citations, name the gaps, and answer the question asked.

quiz.q: A question splits into four independent parts that each need many tool calls. Which design fits best?
choices: One agent with a bigger context window
quiz.why: Independent, read-heavy parts gain from parallel workers with isolated contexts.

quiz.q: Two workers return near-identical findings and one topic is missing. What most likely went wrong?
choices: The workers used too few tokens
quiz.why: Without boundaries workers overlap and the topic nobody owns gets dropped.

quiz.q: A triage agent passes a customer to a billing agent, which then talks to the customer directly. Which pattern is this?
quiz.why: Control and ownership move to one specialist at a time.

quiz.q: What is the main risk of a hierarchical multi-agent system?
choices: Detail fades through each layer of summaries
It cannot run anything in parallel
quiz.why: Every layer summarises, like a game of telephone, and adds cost and latency.

quiz.q: Two parallel workers read a shared list, append one item each and write the whole list back. What happens?
choices: The write fails with an error
quiz.why: The second write replaces the first: a silent lost update.

quiz.q: A worker produced a 20-page result. What should it return to the supervisor?
choices: A short summary and a reference to the stored result
quiz.why: Passing references keeps the supervisor's context small.

quiz.q: Two workers report different prices for the same product from different sources. How should the supervisor merge?
choices: Prefer the newer primary source and mention the conflict
Take the report that arrived last
quiz.why: Resolve on evidence, not arrival order, and keep the citation.

quiz.q: Agents in a network keep passing a task back and forth. What fixes it?
choices: A hop limit, a termination condition and one owner of the answer
quiz.why: Networks need explicit stopping rules and ownership.
